channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Newly identified transport pathway reveals how caveolin-1 helps cells store fat
item.description: Lipodystrophy is a serious metabolic disease characterized by abnormal lipid storage in the body. In people with this condition, ingested fats are not stored in adipose tissue as they are in healthy individuals, but are instead deposited in the liver, muscle tissue or the heart muscle, among other places, with far-reaching metabolic consequences such as fatty liver or type 2 diabetes. The visible redistribution of fat in the body and the other symptoms are very distressing for patients. The causes of the disease may include a congenital gene mutation, an immune disorder or an infection.

item.title: Intermittent fasting helps injured muscles regenerate in mice
item.description: In a new study from Koç University, alternating days of fasting and feeding helped injured muscles regenerate in mice by encouraging repair cells to multiply and fuse into muscle fibers. The effect depended on a molecular pathway previously linked to muscle wasting in cancer.

item.title: 32% of postpartum women report needing mental health care in survey spanning 16 states
item.description: Mental health conditions are the leading cause of pregnancy-related death in the United States. Yet almost all these deaths are considered preventable if women are effectively screened during and after giving birth and then connected with needed care, according to CDC data from 2017–2019.

item.title: New imaging technology reveals previously unseen immune cell patterns in tissue
item.description: Scientists can now see a previously hidden dimension of the immune system thanks to BCR-MERFISH, a new imaging technology developed by researchers at Boston Children's Hospital. By mapping where different groups of antibody-producing cells are located in tissue, the technology could help researchers better understand how immune responses contribute to disease and eventually inform new approaches to diagnosis and treatment. The breakthrough, published in Nature Methods, opens new possibilities for investigating inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune disorders, infections and cancer.

item.title: New structures come into view in brain wiring maps
item.description: Researchers at Harvard Medical School and the University of California San Diego have sped up a powerful imaging technique enough to map, for the first time, large volumes of brain tissue in nanoscale detail. The approach reveals fine structures that brain wiring maps, known as connectomes, can miss.

item.title: Stress and anxiety are wearing workers down: How to spot your triggers and cope
item.description: Workplace stress and anxiety. Who hasn't experienced it?

item.title: Alcohol may weaken cancer immunotherapy, early research suggests
item.description: Cancer immunotherapy has transformed treatment for several advanced cancers, yet the difference between these treatments working and not could depend on simple routine habits. A recent study published in Science Signaling explores one such overlooked factor: regular alcohol consumption.

item.title: Despite soaring demand for GLP-1s, many eligible patients are unable to access these drugs for weight loss
item.description: In just a few short years, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have surged in popularity across the United States, transforming from specialized treatments for type 2 diabetes into revolutionary therapeutics for weight management, cardiovascular health and other emerging uses. But not all populations are benefiting from this expansion. As GLP-1 use has increased, disparities in access to these drugs have widened significantly, according to a new study led by researchers at Boston University School of Public Health (BUSPH).

item.title: Giving patients a greater voice in their diabetes care
item.description: In two related papers published in JAMA Network Open and the Journal of General Internal Medicine, Kasia Lipska, M.D., associate professor of medicine (endocrinology) at Yale School of Medicine (YSM) and her colleagues tested a new approach to incorporating patients' priorities into their diabetes care.

item.title: Upskilling health professionals to deliver emotional well-being support for people with diabetes
item.description: For more than 1.5 million Australians living with diabetes, managing their condition is a relentless, 24-hour responsibility. Day after day, people are required to make decisions about medications, glucose monitoring, food, physical activity and other aspects of their care—largely outside the health care system.

item.title: Major data gap for gut disorders leaves Aotearoa in the dark
item.description: A lack of up-to-date New Zealand research into common gut disorders means the country is effectively flying blind on conditions that may affect about 1 in 3 adults, University of Otago research suggests.

item.title: 'Pan-RAS molecular glue' is a safe and effective treatment for lung and pancreatic cancers
item.description: Results from the AURORAS-1 Phase I clinical trial of an anticancer drug called ERAS-0015 have shown that it is safe and has caused tumors to shrink in hard-to-treat diseases such as lung and pancreatic cancer.

item.title: Mental health diagnoses rise with medical complexity, chronicity in children
item.description: The prevalence of mental health (MH) diagnoses increases with increasing medical complexity and chronicity in Medicaid-enrolled children, according to a study published in Pediatrics.

item.title: Flu vaccine effectiveness often weaker than advertised, study finds
item.description: New research suggests health officials may be overselling the protective power of the annual flu shot—but that doesn't mean folks should skip it, researchers added. The new analysis finds the influenza vaccine is often less protective than the 40% to 60% effectiveness against infection that's routinely stated, according to researchers from the University of Maryland.

item.title: Your genes might boost risk for high cholesterol
item.description: Frustrated that your cholesterol levels aren't budging for the better? You may have your genes to blame, a new study finds.

item.title: Hair pulling, skin picking and nail biting are common in young people and cause significant distress
item.description: The study found that body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs), as they are known, can be a significant source of distress, particularly among young people who also experienced anxiety, depression and bullying.

item.title: Less than half of TikTok videos on RSV prevention offer high-quality info, paper notes
item.description: Many people rely on social media to learn more about health conditions and trends. A study published in Vaccine that examined TikTok videos about respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention—including the maternal vaccine (Abrysvo) and the long-acting antibody nirsevimab (Beyfortus) for infants—finds that only 47% present high-quality information.

item.title: Alcohol addiction and eating disorders often go hand in hand—here's why
item.description: When some people drink, they purposely skip meals in order to amplify the effects of the alcohol or to save calories for their drinks. The practice, sometimes referred to as "drunkorexia," highlights the crossover that can exist between risky drinking behavior and disordered eating.

item.title: Commonly used drug kills leukemia cells early by acting mainly on RNA, not DNA
item.description: For more than two decades, azacitidine has been a major treatment for blood cancers such as high-risk myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The drug was thought to work through DNA, by stripping off the chemical tags that keep genes silenced and allowing those genes to switch back on.

item.title: Researchers uncover the mechanisms of adhesion formation after thoracic surgery
item.description: Intrathoracic adhesions can develop after thoracic surgery and increase the risk of complications during repeat surgery. However, the detailed molecular mechanisms underlying their formation have remained unclear. In a Letter published in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy, a team from Japan aimed to establish an animal model that closely reproduces pleural adhesions seen in patients and to identify key cells and signaling pathways involved in adhesion formation. The goal was to find new methods to prevent adhesions after thoracic surgery.

item.title: Patients give dental implants high marks after 40 years
item.description: Nearly 40 years after receiving dental implants and crowns, patients remain highly satisfied with how well they function. Their views on appearance are more mixed, according to a study from the University of Gothenburg, Sweden.

item.title: Improved mapping reveals location of small molecules in the brain
item.description: Hsi-Chun Chao, a postdoctoral researcher at the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, developed a new methodology to map the locations of and differentiate nearly identical molecules in the brain.

item.title: Metastatic pancreatic cancer responds well to treatment with combination of daraxonrasib and chemotherapy
item.description: Daraxonrasib combined with chemotherapy caused substantial tumor shrinkage in patients with pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body, according to new results from a Phase I/II clinical trial.

item.title: Heart rhythm data reveal early signs of heart disease before conventional measures
item.description: The heart does not beat like a regular clock. Even at rest, the time between successive heartbeats continuously varies. Researchers at Tampere and Stanford universities have shown that the patterns of these subtle variations can reveal the early effects of cardiomyopathy, which is a hereditary heart disease. The paper is published in the journal Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology.

item.title: People respond faster to a sugary drink's logo after three weeks of daily consumption
item.description: You may not love the taste of a certain soda, yet you can still find yourself gravitating toward it when you spot the logo. New discoveries at the Monell Center show that people who drank a labeled, high-sugar beverage for three weeks became more motivated by the drink's logo than by the actual taste of the drink.

item.title: Immune aging blueprint offers new clues to fighting cancer
item.description: A new study from Monash University has uncovered a genetic blueprint of immune aging, shedding light on why our bodies become less effective at fighting cancer and infections as we grow older. Published in Science Immunology, the preclinical study identified genetic changes that cause aging immune cells to become less effective, helping to explain why older people are more susceptible to cancer and experience more frequent and severe infections.

item.title: Nearly half of adults over 70 benefited from exercise training across several areas of physical function
item.description: A yearlong exercise program improved physical function among adults aged over 70, but the benefits varied considerably between individuals. A study conducted at the University of Jyväskylä highlights that the success of exercise interventions should not be evaluated using a single outcome measure, as positive changes may occur in different aspects of physical function.

item.title: Cell biologists uncover key mechanism behind a rare cause of childhood epilepsy
item.description: University of Liverpool scientists have discovered how a protein linked to a severe form of childhood epilepsy is positioned within nerve cells, providing new insights into a rare genetic neurological disorder.

item.title: Inner ear study challenges canonical understanding of hearing
item.description: New research offers a new understanding of how the inner ear processes sound, which could lead to improvements in hearing technology like cochlear implants.

item.title: Can psychedelics improve decision-making?
item.description: For the one-in-five Americans with a mental health condition, the options for treatment aren't too much different from what they were half a century ago. Most medicines for psychiatric disorders were first pioneered in the 1950s.
